payload.rationale: The latest observed Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year rate is 6.95% (Sep 17, 2026), after a sharp 19 bp weekly jump from 6.76%. Resolution YES requires the Sep 24 print to be at least 7.02% (published to two decimals), i.e., a further rise of about 7 bps or more. Historically, week-to-week PMMS changes have a standard deviation of roughly 10-13 bps with little persistent drift, so a +7 bp move is somewhat less likely than not but far from rare. Because the PMMS is a weekly average of daily rates, a large jump often means end-of-week daily rates were above the weekly mean, which gives modest positive carryover into the next week; this argues for a slightly higher probability than a naive zero-mean random walk. Balancing these, I estimate roughly a 30% chance. Too high: large weekly jumps frequently partially reverse (mean reversion after rate spikes), and the threshold sits 6-7 bps above the current level, so a flat or down week resolves NO. Too low: if the recent surge reflects an ongoing bond-yield selloff (e.g., hawkish Fed repricing or inflation surprise), rates could keep climbing and end-of-week daily rates may already be near or above 7%, making a 7.02%+ weekly average quite plausible. No Treasury/MBS yield or daily lender-rate data are available to resolve this.
limitations: Only five weekly PMMS observations supplied; no daily rate, 10-year Treasury, or MBS spread data to gauge momentum after the Sep 17 jump.
Weekly change distribution is assumed from general historical behavior, not fitted to current volatility regime.
Unknown macro catalysts (Fed communications, inflation data) in the Sep 18-24 window could move rates sharply in either direction.
Rounding/publication conventions assumed standard (two decimals, first published value).
